verses.36:14: He set them on the shoulder pieces of the ephod as stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
verses.36:15: He made the breastpiece as the work of a skilled designer, like the work of the ephod, of gold, blue, purple, and crimson yarn, and twisted fine linen.
verses.36:16: It was square; they made the breastpiece folded double, a span in its length and a span in its width when folded double.
verses.36:17: They set in it four rows of stones: a row of carnelian, topaz, and emerald was the first row.
verses.36:18: The second row was turquoise, lapis lazuli, and rock crystal.
verses.36:19: The third row was jacinth, agate, and amethyst.
verses.36:20: And the fourth row was chrysolite, onyx, and jasper; they were enclosed in gold filigree settings in their mountings.
verses.36:21: The stones corresponded to the names of the sons of Israel, twelve of them according to their names, like the engravings of a signet, each according to his name, for the twelve tribes.
verses.36:22: They made on the breastpiece braided chains of corded work, of pure gold.
verses.36:23: They made two gold filigree settings and two gold rings, and they placed the two rings on the two ends of the breastpiece.
verses.36:24: Then they put the two gold cords onto the two rings at the ends of the breastpiece.
verses.36:25: The two ends of the two cords they put onto the two filigree settings, and they placed them on the shoulder pieces of the ephod at its front.
verses.36:26: They made two gold rings and set them on the two ends of the breastpiece, on its edge facing the ephod on the inside.
verses.36:27: They made two gold rings and placed them on the two shoulder pieces of the ephod below, at its front, right beside its seam, above the woven band of the ephod.
verses.36:28: They tied the breastpiece by its rings to the rings of the ephod with a blue cord, so that it would rest upon the woven band of the ephod and the breastpiece would not come loose from the ephod, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
verses.36:29: He made the robe of the ephod, the work of a weaver, entirely of blue.
verses.36:30: The opening of the robe was in its center, like the opening of a coat of mail, with an edging around its opening so that it would not tear.
verses.36:31: On the hem of the robe they made pomegranates of twisted blue, purple, and crimson yarn.
verses.36:32: They made bells of pure gold and placed the bells between the pomegranates all around the hem of the robe, between the pomegranates.
verses.36:33: A bell and a pomegranate, a bell and a pomegranate, all around the hem of the robe for ministering, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
verses.36:34: They made the tunics of fine linen, the work of a weaver, for Aaron and for his sons,
verses.36:35: and the turban of fine linen, and the ornate caps of fine linen, and the linen undergarments of twisted fine linen,
verses.36:36: and the sash of twisted fine linen, and blue, purple, and crimson yarn, the work of an embroiderer, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
verses.36:37: They made the plate of the holy diadem of pure gold, and they inscribed on it an inscription like the engravings of a signet: "Holiness to the LORD."
verses.36:38: They put a blue cord on it to place it high on the turban, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.
verses.37:1: All the wise-hearted among those doing the work made the tabernacle of ten curtains of twisted fine linen, and blue, purple, and crimson yarn; with cherubim, the work of a skilled designer, he made them.
verses.37:2: The length of each curtain was twenty-eight cubits, and the width of each curtain was four cubits; all the curtains were of one measurement.
verses.37:3: He made the veil of blue, purple, and crimson yarn, and twisted fine linen; as the work of a skilled designer he made it with cherubim.
verses.37:4: He made for it four pillars of acacia wood and overlaid them with gold; their hooks were of gold, and he cast for them four bases of silver.
verses.37:5: He made a screen for the entrance of the tent of blue, purple, and crimson yarn, and twisted fine linen, the work of an embroiderer,
verses.37:6: and its five pillars with their hooks; he overlaid their tops and their bands with gold, and their five bases were of bronze.
verses.37:7: He made the courtyard. For the south side, facing southward, the hangings of the courtyard were of twisted fine linen, one hundred cubits.
verses.37:8: Their pillars were twenty and their bases were twenty, of bronze; the hooks of the pillars and their bands were of silver.
verses.37:9: And for the north side, one hundred cubits; their pillars were twenty and their bases were twenty, of bronze; the hooks of the pillars and their bands were of silver.
verses.37:10: And for the west side, hangings of fifty cubits; their pillars were ten and their bases were ten; the hooks of the pillars and their bands were of silver.
verses.37:11: And for the east side, facing eastward, fifty cubits.
verses.37:12: The hangings for the one flank were fifteen cubits; their pillars were three and their bases were three.
verses.37:13: And for the second flank, on this side and on that side of the gate of the courtyard, the hangings were fifteen cubits; their pillars were three and their bases were three.
verses.37:14: All the hangings of the courtyard all around were of twisted fine linen.
verses.37:15: The bases for the pillars were of bronze, the hooks of the pillars and their bands were of silver, and the overlaying of their tops was of silver; and all the pillars of the courtyard were banded with silver.
verses.37:16: The screen for the gate of the courtyard was the work of an embroiderer, of blue, purple, and crimson yarn, and twisted fine linen; it was twenty cubits in length, and the height in width was five cubits, matching the hangings of the courtyard.
verses.37:17: Their pillars were four and their bases were four, of bronze; their hooks were of silver, and the overlaying of their tops and their bands were of silver.
verses.37:18: All the pegs for the tabernacle and for the courtyard all around were of bronze.
verses.37:19: These are the records of the tabernacle, the tabernacle of the testimony, as it was recorded at the command of Moses—the service of the Levites under the hand of Ithamar, son of Aaron the priest.
verses.37:20: Now Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, made everything that the LORD had commanded Moses.
verses.37:21: And with him was Oholiab, son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, an artisan, a skilled designer, and an embroiderer in blue, in purple, in crimson, and in fine linen.
verses.38:1: Then Bezalel made the ark of acacia wood: two and a half cubits was its length, one and a half cubits its width, and one and a half cubits its height.
verses.38:2: He overlaid it with pure gold on the inside and on the outside, and he made for it a molding of gold all around.
verses.38:3: He cast for it four gold rings on its four feet, two rings on its one side and two rings on its other side.
verses.38:4: And he inserted the poles into the rings on the sides of the ark to carry the ark.
verses.38:5: He made an atonement cover of pure gold: two and a half cubits was its length, and one and a half cubits its width.
verses.38:6: He made two cherubim of gold; of hammered work he made them, at the two ends of the atonement cover.
verses.38:7: One cherub was at the end on one side and one cherub at the end on the other side; out of the atonement cover he made the cherubim at its two ends.
verses.38:8: The cherubim had their wings spread upward, shielding the atonement cover with their wings, and their faces were toward one another; toward the atonement cover were the faces of the cherubim.
verses.38:9: Then he made the table of acacia wood: two cubits was its length, one cubit its width, and one and a half cubits its height.
verses.38:10: He cast for it four gold rings and placed the rings on the four corners that belonged to its four legs. Alongside the rim were the rings, as holders for the poles to carry the table.
verses.38:11: He made poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with gold. And he made the poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with gold to carry the table.
verses.38:12: He made the utensils that were on the table of pure gold: its platters, its ladles, its bowls, and the pitchers with which drink offerings were to be poured.
verses.38:13: He made the lampstand of pure gold. Of hammered work he made the lampstand, its base and its shaft; its cups, its bulbs, and its flowers were one piece with it.
verses.38:15: And six branches extended from its sides: three lampstand branches from its one side and three lampstand branches from its other side.
verses.38:16: There were three cups shaped like almond blossoms on the one branch, with a bulb and a flower, and three cups shaped like almond blossoms on the other branch, with a bulb and a flower; so it was for the six branches extending from the lampstand. Their bulbs and their branches were one piece with it; all of it was a single hammered piece of pure gold.
verses.38:17: He made its seven lamps, and its tongs and its firepans, of pure gold.
verses.38:18: He overlaid the planks with gold and made their rings of gold as holders for the bars, and he overlaid the bars with gold.
verses.38:22: Then he made the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood: five cubits was its length and five cubits its width—it was square—and three cubits its height.
verses.38:23: He made all the utensils of the altar: the pots, the shovels, the sprinkling bowls, the forks, and the firepans; all its utensils he made of bronze.
verses.38:24: He made for the altar a grating of bronze meshwork, beneath its ledge from below to its midpoint. And he cast four rings at the four corners of the bronze grating as holders for the poles.
verses.38:25: He made the holy anointing oil and the pure incense of spices, the work of a perfumer.
verses.38:26: He made the bronze basin and its bronze stand from the mirrors of the serving women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting.
verses.38:27: And from it Moses and Aaron and his sons would wash their hands and their feet. Whenever they entered the tent of meeting and when they approached the altar, they would wash, just as the LORD commanded Moses.
verses.39:1: All the gold used for the work, in all the work of the sanctuary—the gold of the wave offering—came to twenty-nine talents and seven hundred and thirty shekels, by the shekel of the sanctuary.
verses.39:2: And the silver from those registered of the congregation was one hundred talents and one thousand, seven hundred and seventy-five shekels, by the shekel of the sanctuary.
verses.39:3: A beka per head—half a shekel by the shekel of the sanctuary—for everyone who passed over to those registered, from twenty years old and upward, for six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty.
verses.39:4: And the one hundred talents of silver were used for casting the bases of the sanctuary and the bases of the veil—one hundred bases for the one hundred talents, one talent per base.
verses.39:5: And from the one thousand, seven hundred and seventy-five shekels he made hooks for the pillars, overlaid their tops, and fitted them with bands.
verses.39:6: And the bronze of the wave offering was seventy talents and two thousand, four hundred shekels.
verses.39:8: And the bases of the courtyard all around, the bases of the gate of the courtyard, all the pegs of the tabernacle, and all the pegs of the courtyard all around.
verses.39:9: With it he made the bases of the entrance of the tent of meeting, the bronze altar, the bronze grating that belonged to it, and all the utensils of the altar.
verses.39:10: So all the work of the tabernacle of the tent of meeting was finished; the sons of Israel did according to everything that the LORD commanded Moses, just so they did.
verses.39:13: Then they brought the tabernacle to Moses: the tent and all its furnishings, its clasps, its planks, its bars, its pillars, and its bases;
verses.39:14: the ark of the testimony, its poles, and the atonement cover;
verses.39:15: the gold altar, the anointing oil, the incense of spices, and the screen for the entrance of the tent;
verses.39:16: the pure lampstand, its lamps—the lamps arranged in order—all its utensils, and the oil for the light;
verses.39:17: the table, all of its utensils, and the bread of the Presence;
verses.39:18: the finely woven garments for ministering in the sanctuary, the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and the garments of his sons for serving as priests;
verses.39:19: the courtyard hangings, its pillars and its bases, the screen for the courtyard gate, its ropes and its pegs, and all the furnishings for the service of the tabernacle, for the tent of meeting;
verses.39:20: and the covering of ram skins dyed red, the covering of fine leather skins, and the screening veil.
verses.39:22: According to everything that the LORD commanded Moses, so the sons of Israel did all the work.
verses.39:23: And Moses saw all the work, and look, they had done it; just as the LORD commanded, so they had done. And Moses blessed them.
verses.40:1: Now the LORD spoke to Moses, saying,
verses.40:2: "On the day of the first month, on the first of the month, you shall set up the tabernacle of the tent of meeting.
verses.40:3: You shall place the ark of the testimony there, and screen the ark with the curtain.
verses.40:4: You shall bring in the table and lay out its arrangement, and bring in the lampstand and light its lamps.
verses.40:5: You shall put the gold altar for incense in front of the ark of the testimony, and place the screen for the entrance of the tabernacle.
verses.40:6: You shall put the altar of burnt offering in front of the entrance of the tabernacle of the tent of meeting.
verses.40:8: You shall place the courtyard all around, and put up the screen of the courtyard gate.
verses.40:9: You shall take the anointing oil and anoint the tabernacle and everything that is in it, and consecrate it and all its articles, and it will be holy.
verses.40:10: And you shall anoint the altar of burnt offering and all its articles, and consecrate the altar, and the altar will be most holy.
verses.40:12: You shall bring Aaron and his sons near to the entrance of the tent of meeting, and wash them with water.
verses.40:13: You shall clothe Aaron with the holy garments, and anoint him and consecrate him, so that he may serve as a priest to Me.
verses.40:14: And you shall bring his sons near and clothe them with tunics.
verses.40:15: You shall anoint them just as you anointed their father, so that they may serve as priests to Me; and their anointing is to be for them an everlasting priesthood throughout their generations."
verses.40:16: So Moses did; in accordance with everything that the LORD commanded him, so he did.
verses.40:17: It happened in the first month, in the second year, on the first of the month, that the tabernacle was set up.
verses.40:18: Moses set up the tabernacle: he put down its bases, placed its frames, put in its crossbars, and set up its pillars.
verses.40:19: He spread out the tent over the tabernacle and placed the covering of the tent over it on top, just as the LORD commanded Moses.
verses.40:20: He took the testimony and put it into the ark, placed the poles on the ark, and put the atonement cover on the ark above.
verses.40:21: He brought the ark into the tabernacle, placed the screening curtain, and screened the ark of the testimony, just as the LORD commanded Moses.
verses.40:22: He put the table in the tent of meeting, on the side of the tabernacle toward the north, outside the curtain.
verses.40:23: He laid out an arrangement of bread on it before the LORD, just as the LORD commanded Moses.
verses.40:24: He placed the lampstand in the tent of meeting, opposite the table, on the side of the tabernacle toward the south.
verses.40:25: And he lit the lamps before the LORD, just as the LORD commanded Moses.
verses.40:26: He placed the gold altar in the tent of meeting, in front of the curtain.
verses.40:27: And he burned aromatic incense on it, just as the LORD commanded Moses.
verses.40:29: And he placed the altar of burnt offering at the entrance of the tabernacle of the tent of meeting, and offered up the burnt offering and the grain offering on it, just as the LORD commanded Moses.
verses.40:33: He set up the courtyard all around the tabernacle and the altar, and put up the screen of the courtyard gate. And Moses completed the work.
verses.40:34: Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, while the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.
verses.40:35: And Moses was unable to go into the tent of meeting, because the cloud rested on it and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.
verses.40:36: And whenever the cloud was lifted up from above the tabernacle, the sons of Israel would break camp throughout all their journeys.
verses.40:37: But if the cloud was not lifted up, then they would not break camp until the day it was lifted up.
verses.40:38: For the cloud of the LORD was over the tabernacle by day, and fire would be in it by night, before the eyes of the whole house of Israel throughout all their journeys.

notes.1:7: Hebrew wayyishretsu (Qal of sh-r-ts) literally means "teemed" or "swarmed," echoing the abundant multiplication of living creatures in Genesis 1 and 9:7.
notes.1:14: The Hebrew construction avdu bahem (Qal of avad with the preposition b-) is a technical idiom meaning to exact forced labor from someone, paired here and in v. 13 with bepharekh, "with brutality" or "ruthlessly."
notes.1:16: Hebrew ha'ovnayim is a dual noun literally meaning "the two stones," referring to the birthing stones or birthstool on which a woman crouched during delivery.
notes.1:19: Hebrew chayot ("vigorous" or "lively") plays on the verb chayah ("live" or "keep alive") repeated throughout vv. 16-22.
notes.1:22: Following the Masoretic Text strictly, Pharaoh says "Every son who is born," without the added phrase "to the Hebrews" found in the Samaritan Pentateuch and Septuagint.
notes.2:2: Hebrew ki-tov hu ("that he was good") uses the same wording as Genesis 1:4, conveying wholeness, beauty, and delight.
notes.2:3: Hebrew tevah ("basket," an Egyptian loanword meaning chest or box) is the same word used for Noah's ark in Genesis 6-9.
notes.2:10: The name Moses (Mosheh) is linked by wordplay to the Hebrew verb mashah ("draw out"), while also corresponding to the Egyptian element meaning "child" or "born of."
notes.2:22: The name Gershom plays on the Hebrew words ger ("sojourner") and sham ("there").
notes.2:25: Hebrew wayyeda elohim ("and God knew") uses the verb yada absolutely without a stated object, expressing deep personal awareness and concern.
notes.3:14: Hebrew Ehyeh asher ehyeh ("I WILL BE WHO I WILL BE") uses the Qal imperfect of hayah ("be"), echoing "I will be with you" in v. 12; it is also widely rendered timelessly as "I AM WHO I AM" and connects by wordplay to the divine name YHWH ("the LORD") in v. 15.
notes.3:16: Hebrew paqod paqadti pairs the Qal infinitive absolute and perfect of paqad ("attend to," "visit," or "take careful notice of") for emphasis, echoing Joseph's final words in Genesis 50:24-25.
notes.3:19: The Masoretic Text reads literally velo beyad chazaqah ("and not by a strong hand," i.e., not even when faced with a strong hand), whereas the Septuagint reads "unless by a mighty hand."
notes.3:22: Hebrew venitsaltem is the Piel of natsal ("strip" or "plunder"), forming an ironic wordplay with the Hiphil of the same root in v. 8 (lehattsilo, "to rescue them").
notes.4:2: The written form (ketiv) coalesces the two words as one (mzh), while the read form (qere), translated here, divides them as mah-zeh ("what is this").
notes.4:13: Literally "send now by the hand of [whom] You will send," an elliptical construct phrase before a finite verb (tishlach) expressing Moses's reluctance and asking God to send someone else.
notes.4:18: The Masoretic Text gives the shorter form of the name, Jether (yeter), in the first clause and the fuller form, Jethro (yitro), in the second.
notes.4:21: The Hebrew verb (achazzeq, Piel of chazaq) literally means "strengthen" or "make firm," used with "heart" to signify making Pharaoh resolute and obstinate.
notes.4:25: The masculine pronouns in vv. 24-26 leave unspecified whether the LORD confronted Moses or his son, and "feet" (raglayw) may be a Hebrew euphemism for the genitals. The difficult expression "bridegroom of blood" (chatan-damim) links the blood of circumcision to a covenantal or protective rite.
notes.5:3: The verb "has met" (niqra) is a Niphal perfect spelled with aleph for the III-He root qarah ("meet, encounter"), referring to a divine encounter.
notes.5:12: The Hebrew pairs a Poel infinitive construct with a cognate noun, leqoshesh qash ("to gather stubble"), vivid wordplay highlighting the Israelites' desperate scavenging.
notes.5:16: The Masoretic vocalization wechatat is a rare third-person feminine singular Qal perfect of chata ("sin, be at fault") with "your people" (ammeka) as subject, indicating that Pharaoh's own Egyptian officials are to blame rather than the Israelite laborers.
notes.5:23: Hebrew pairs the Hiphil infinitive absolute with the negated finite verb (hatstsel lo-hitstsalta, from natsal) for strong emphasis ("not rescued at all"), while the Hiphil of raa ("caused harm") echoes Moses's question to the LORD in v. 22.
notes.6:3: The preposition be- before El Shaddai ("God Almighty") is a beth essentiae ("as / in the capacity of"). The phrase "My name, the LORD" stands in casus pendens (or adverbial specification) before the Niphal perfect noda'ti (root yd'), which may be understood passively ("I was not known") or reflexively ("I did not make Myself known").
notes.6:8: "Lifted My hand" renders the literal Hebrew idiom nasati et-yadi, a gesture accompanying a solemn oath.
notes.6:9: "Shortness of spirit" translates the Hebrew idiom qotser ruach (literally "shortness of spirit/breath"), denoting exhaustion, anguish, or despondency.
notes.6:12: "Uncircumcised of lips" translates the Hebrew idiom aral sefatayim (repeated in 6:30), denoting speech that is impeded, awkward, or unpersuasive.
notes.7:1: Hebrew netattika elohim literally means "I have given/made you God," using natan ("give/appoint") with a double accusative to designate Moses as God's authoritative representative before Pharaoh, with Aaron acting as his prophetic spokesman.
notes.7:13: Exodus 7 uses three distinct Hebrew roots for Pharaoh's obduracy: qashah in the Hiphil ("make hard/stiff," 7:3), chazaq in the intransitive Qal ("grow hard/strong," 7:13, 22), and the stative kaved (literally "heavy," i.e., "unyielding," 7:14).
notes.7:17: The phrase "in My hand" (beyadi) continues the LORD's first-person oracle ("I am about to strike," anoki makkeh), attributing the action of His human agent holding the staff (7:15, 19-20) directly to Himself (cf. 7:25).
notes.7:19: Hebrew uba'etsim uba'avanim (literally "in the woods and in the stones," i.e., "in wood and in stone") refers to water held in wooden and stone containers.
notes.7:26: Verses 7:26-29 follow the Masoretic versification, corresponding to 8:1-4 in most English versions.
notes.8:5: The Hithpael imperative of פאר ("Take the honor over me") is a polite idiom by which Moses grants Pharaoh the privilege of specifying the time for the frogs to be removed.
notes.8:11: The Hiphil infinitive absolute הַכְבֵּד ("made heavy") continues the narrative sequence of the preceding finite verb. Throughout Exodus 8-9, כבד ("make/become heavy," 8:11, 28; 9:7, 34) is kept distinct from חזק ("grow/make hard," 8:15; 9:12, 35) and echoes the "heavy" (כָּבֵד) plagues.
notes.8:17: The Hebrew pairs two stems of the root שׁלח: Piel מְשַׁלֵּחַ ("send away") and Hiphil מַשְׁלִיחַ ("send [against]"). The collective noun עָרֹב denotes a dense swarm of biting insects or flies.
notes.8:19: The Masoretic Hebrew reads פְדֻת ("redemption, deliverance"), portraying a redeeming separation between Israel and Egypt, whereas ancient versions such as the Septuagint render it more generally as "division" or "distinction."
notes.8:27: The verb form וַיָּסַר (from סור) can be parsed either as Qal ("departed," matching Moses's Qal verb in 8:25 and lacking the object marker אֶת) or as Hiphil ("He removed").
notes.9:3: The form הוֹיָה is a rare Qal feminine participle of the archaic root הוה (a by-form of היה, "to be"), the only such participle of this verb in the Hebrew Bible, expressing imminent action ("is coming").
notes.9:15: The construction כִּי עַתָּה followed by a perfect verb (שָׁלַחְתִּי) and waw-consecutive forms expresses a counterfactual past condition ("by now I could have... and you would have been wiped out").
notes.9:16: The Hiphil verb הֶעֱמַדְתִּיךָ (from עמד, "stand") literally means "I have caused you to stand" or "kept you standing," contrasting with being wiped out in 9:15. The Piel infinitive construct סַפֵּר has an indefinite subject ("be recounted").
notes.9:17: The rare Hithpoel participle מִסְתּוֹלֵל (from סלל, "heap up a mound," with metathesis of ת and ס) vividly portrays Pharaoh raising himself up as a barrier against God's people.
notes.9:31: The agricultural terms גִּבְעֹל ("in bud," 9:31) and אֲפִילֹת ("ripen late," 9:32) are hapax legomena in the Hebrew Bible; כֻּסֶּמֶת (9:32) refers to emmer wheat, a late-ripening grain cultivated in Egypt.
notes.10:1: The Hiphil verb הִכְבַּדְתִּי ("made heavy") depicts Pharaoh's heart as dull and unresponsive, distinct from the Piel verb חִזֵּק ("strengthened/hardened") in 10:20, 27 and 11:10. The Masoretic singular suffix in בְּקִרְבּוֹ ("in his midst") refers to Pharaoh or his realm.
notes.10:5: "The surface of the land" translates the Hebrew idiom עֵין הָאָרֶץ, literally "the eye of the land" (also in 10:15).
notes.10:10: Pharaoh's opening clause is a sarcastic imprecation ("So may the LORD be with you, just as..."). The idiom רָעָה נֶגֶד פְּנֵיכֶם ("evil is right before your face") can mean either that they harbor evil intentions or that disaster awaits them directly ahead.
notes.10:19: Hebrew רוּחַ־יָם (literally "sea wind") denotes a west wind blowing from the Mediterranean. יָמָּה סּוּף is literally "to the Sea of Reeds," traditionally rendered "the Red Sea" following the Septuagint.
notes.10:21: וְיָמֵשׁ חֹשֶׁךְ ("darkness one can feel") uses an impersonal Hiphil jussive of the root מושׁ (a by-form of משׁשׁ, "to feel/grope"), literally "so that one may feel darkness."
notes.11:1: The adverbial noun כָּלָה ("completely/altogether") may modify either "when he lets you go" or the following emphatic Piel infinitive absolute construction גָּרֵשׁ יְגָרֵשׁ ("he will surely drive out").
notes.11:6: In the Masoretic Text, the masculine singular suffix in כָּמֹהוּ ("the like of it," twice) refers back to the grammatically feminine noun צְעָקָה ("outcry"), while the verbs נִהְיָתָה (Niphal) and תֹסִף (Hiphil) remain feminine singular.
notes.11:7: The idiom לֹא יֶחֱרַץ־כֶּלֶב לְשֹׁנוֹ (literally "not a dog will sharpen its tongue") expresses total absence of hostility, meaning not even a dog will snarl or bark against them (compare Josh 10:21).
notes.11:8: The phrase אֲשֶׁר־בְּרַגְלֶיךָ (literally "who are at your feet") is a Hebrew idiom for followers under someone's leadership. The direct quotation of the LORD's words ends at verse 7, with verse 8 resuming Moses' own address to Pharaoh.
notes.12:3: Hebrew "seh" denotes a single individual animal from the flock, either a sheep or a goat, as verse 5 clarifies.
notes.12:6: "At twilight" renders the literal Hebrew dual idiom "ben ha-arbayim" ("between the two evenings"), variously understood as the period between afternoon and sunset or between sunset and full dark.
notes.12:22: Hebrew "saf" can mean either "basin" or "threshold"; translating "basin" follows its use for a vessel holding liquids, though some ancient versions and interpreters understand the blood as held at the doorway threshold.
notes.12:40: The Masoretic Text states simply "in Egypt"; the Samaritan Pentateuch and Septuagint expand the phrase to include the patriarchs' stay in the land of Canaan.
notes.12:42: Hebrew "shimmurim" (an intensive plural noun from "shamar," to watch or keep) carries a double resonance here: the LORD's own protective vigil on the night of the exodus, and Israel's ongoing night of observance through every generation.
notes.13:8: Hebrew literally reads ba'avur zeh asah YHWH li ("on account of this [which] the LORD did for me"), with the demonstrative zeh introducing an elliptical relative clause explaining the observance.
notes.13:10: Literally "from days to days" (miyyamim yamimah), a Hebrew idiom denoting an annual cycle.
notes.13:17: The particle ki functions concessively ("although/even though"). The Hebrew also plays on sound between naham (Qal of nhh, "led them") and yinnahem (Niphal of nhm, "change their minds/regret").
notes.13:18: Hebrew yam-suph literally means "Sea of Reeds." The Qal passive participle hamushim ("equipped for battle" or "in battle array") is a rare military term of debated etymology (cf. Josh 1:14; 4:12; Judg 7:11).
notes.13:22: The Hiphil imperfect yamish (from mush) is rendered intransitively ("did not withdraw"), though it can also be read transitively with the LORD as implied subject ("He did not remove").
notes.14:11: Hebrew stacks two negatives, hamibbeli ein (lit. "from lack of there-not-being"), for emphatic sarcasm.
notes.14:13: Hebrew asher re'item et-mitsrayim can be read adverbially ("the way you have seen the Egyptians," contrasting with seeing them dead in v. 30) or relatively ("the Egyptians whom you have seen").
notes.14:20: Translates the Masoretic text directly (wayhi he'anan wehahoshekh wayya'er et-hallaylah), which concisely captures the cloud's dual effect of darkness and illumination without harmonizing to ancient versions.
notes.14:25: The Masoretic text reads wayyasar (Hiphil of sur, "removed" or "turned aside"), rather than the Samaritan/Septuagint variant "bound/clogged." The noun kevedut ("difficulty/heaviness") shares the root k-v-d with the LORD's "winning glory" in vv. 4, 17, and 18.
notes.14:27: Hebrew etan denotes a perennial, steady flow or normal state of water, and the Piel wayna'er (from na'ar) vividly pictures the LORD shaking the Egyptians off into the sea (cf. Ps 136:15).
notes.15:2: Hebrew uses the shortened poetic divine name Yah and the form zimrat, 'song' (or possibly 'might/defense'), sharing the first-person possessive force of 'my strength.' The verb rendered 'I will glorify Him' is a hapax legomenon Hiphil of navah, meaning 'glorify/beautify' or possibly 'prepare a dwelling for.'
notes.15:4: Hebrew yam-suph literally means 'Sea of Reeds' (so also in 15:22), traditionally known as the Red Sea following the Septuagint.
notes.15:6: The Niphal participle ne'dari ('majestic') carries the archaic poetic linking vowel known as hireq compaginis.
notes.15:25: Hebrew uses masculine singular pronominal suffixes ('for him,' 'tested him') referring collectively to the people of Israel, which is grammatically singular.
notes.16:2: Ketiv reads the Hiphil wayyallinu while the Masoretic Qere reads the Niphal wayyillonu, both meaning 'they grumbled'; the translation follows the Qere.
notes.16:7: Ketiv reads the Niphal tillonu while the Masoretic Qere reads the Hiphil tallinu, both meaning 'you grumble'; the translation follows the Qere.
notes.16:14: Hebrew mechuspas is a hapax legomenon quadrilateral passive participle, understood from Semitic cognates to mean 'flaky' or 'scale-like.'
notes.16:15: Hebrew man hu uses a rare dialectal or Aramaizing interrogative ('What is it?'), creating a wordplay with the name man ('manna') in 16:31.
notes.16:20: Hebrew wayyarum is a hapax verb meaning 'teem with worms' or 'breed worms,' related to the noun rimmah ('maggots') in 16:24.
notes.17:7: The place names echo the verbs in v. 2 and v. 7: Massah derives from nasah (Piel, 'to test'), and Meribah derives from rib (Qal, 'to contend').
notes.17:12: Hebrew literally reads 'and his hands were steadiness' (using the feminine singular noun emunah with a singular verb), expressing that Moses' hands remained steadily upheld.
notes.17:16: Hebrew reads 'upon the kes of Yah,' using a rare shortened form of kisse ('throne') paired with the shortened divine name Yah. The idiom 'a hand upon the throne of the LORD' is understood either as a solemn oath gesture or as Amalek's hostile hand raised against God's throne.
notes.18:2: The phrase 'after she had been sent away' translates achar shillucheiha, from the plural verbal noun shilluchim (related to Piel shalach, 'to send away'), which leaves unspecified when or why Moses had sent Zipporah back to Midian.
notes.18:6: The Masoretic Text literally reads 'And he said to Moses,' expressing idiomatically that Jethro sent word ahead to Moses before Moses went out to meet him in v. 7.
notes.18:11: The final clause is syntactically elliptical in Hebrew (literally 'for in the matter in which they acted arrogantly against them'), implying that the LORD proved His supremacy over Egypt precisely in the arrogance they displayed against Israel.
notes.18:20: The verb 'teach' translates Hiphil zahar (vehizhartah), which normally carries the stronger sense of 'warn' or 'admonish' and here denotes careful, solemn instruction in God's statutes and instructions.
notes.19:5: The noun segullah ('special treasure') designates a king's private, prized possession, denoting Israel's unique status as the LORD's own treasured people.
notes.19:13: The phrase 'when the ram's horn sounds a long blast' translates bimshokh hayyovel (literally 'at the drawing out of the ram's horn'), referring to a prolonged signal blast; 'stoned' and 'shot through' both employ emphatic infinitive-absolute plus Niphal imperfect constructions.
notes.19:19: Hebrew bekol literally means 'with a voice' or 'with a sound,' understood either as an audible voice so the people could hear (as promised in v. 9) or as thunder echoing v. 16.
notes.19:25: Hebrew vayyomer alehem ('and he said to them') unusually concludes without quoting Moses' words, indicating succinctly that he relayed the LORD's warning to the people.
notes.20:13: The Hebrew source here orders verses 13-15 as adultery (tin'af), theft (tignov), and murder (tirtsach), matching the sequence attested in the Nash Papyrus and Codex Vaticanus of the Septuagint, whereas the standard Masoretic Text orders them murder, adultery, theft.
notes.20:18: Hebrew literally says the people were seeing (Qal participle ro'im) both visible phenomena and sounds, using "see" in a broad sense of sensory perception; likewise the Masoretic verb wayyar' ("and saw") is followed rather than the Septuagint reading "feared."
notes.20:23: The Masoretic pause (atnah) falls after "alongside Me" (itti), creating an elliptical opening clause whose implied object ("gods") is supplied from the following "gods of silver or gods of gold."
notes.20:25: Hebrew cherev ordinarily means "sword," but here denotes a metal stone-cutting tool or chisel; the Hiphil perfect henafta ("swing") with the following Piel wayyiqtol ("profane") expresses a conditional consequence.
notes.21:6: Hebrew ha'elohim literally means "God," pointing to a solemn legal ratification before God, though ancient Jewish tradition and some translations understand it as "the judges."
notes.21:8: Ketiv/Qere: the written text (ketiv) reads lo' ("not," i.e., "whom he has not designated"), whereas the read text (qere) translated here reads lo ("for himself," i.e., "whom he designated for himself").
notes.21:10: Hebrew onatah is a hapax legomenon (occurring only here in the Hebrew Bible); it is traditionally rendered "her marital rights," though some lexicographers propose "oil / ointments" or "dwelling."
notes.21:16: The Hebrew source here places cursing one's parents in v. 16 and kidnapping in v. 17, matching the sequence of the Septuagint, whereas the standard Masoretic Text places kidnapping in v. 16 and cursing one's parents in v. 17.
notes.21:22: Hebrew weyatse'u yeladeyha literally means "and her children come out," leaving open whether premature live birth or miscarriage is envisioned; biphlilim ("as assessed by the judges") derives from the judicial root pll.
notes.22:4: Hebrew uses two stems of the root ba'ar (Hiphil 'cause to be grazed' and Piel 'graze'), playing on the cognate noun be'ir ('livestock,' spelled with the archaic 3ms suffix -oh) and anticipating the homonymous root ba'ar ('burn') in 22:5.
notes.22:8: Both occurrences of 'God' translate elohim (with the definite article in the first clause), which in the second clause takes a 3mp Hiphil imperfect verb (yarshi'un, 'declare guilty'). While some ancient and traditional interpretations understand elohim here and in 22:7 as human judges, the literal rendering 'God' aligns with the oath before the LORD in 22:10.
notes.22:14: The terse Hebrew idiom ba bisekharo (literally 'it came in its hire') means that any risk of injury or death was already covered by the rental fee paid for the hired animal.
notes.22:28: Literally 'your fullness and your tear/dripping'; mele'ah denotes the full yield of harvested grain, while the rare noun dema' (occurring only here in the Hebrew Bible) refers metaphorically to the pressed liquid juice of wine and olive oil.
notes.23:2: Hebrew plays on two stems of the root natah ('turn/incline'): the Qal infinitive construct lintot ('to turn aside' after the many) and the Hiphil infinitive construct lehattot ('to bend/pervert' justice, with the object 'justice' implied from the parallel Hiphil verb in 23:6).
notes.23:5: Hebrew pairs two verbs from homonymous roots 'azav: 'azav I ('leave, abandon') with 'to him,' followed by an emphatic Qal infinitive absolute and imperfect of 'azav II ('free, release, help') with 'with him.' Alternatively, 'you must hold back' can be read as continuing the conditional clause ('and you would refrain from helping him, you must certainly help him').
notes.23:17: Hebrew reads ha'adon YHWH ('the Sovereign, the LORD'), using the definite singular noun ha'adon rather than the usual 'adonai before the Tetragrammaton.
notes.23:25: The Masoretic Hebrew shifts in mid-verse from third-person singular ('and He will bless,' referring to the LORD your God) back to first-person singular ('and I will remove'), a change preserved here without harmonizing to the ancient versions.
notes.23:28: The collective feminine singular noun hatsir'ah is traditionally rendered 'the hornets' (also in Deut 7:20 and Josh 24:12), though some lexicographers relate it to a Semitic root meaning 'panic' or 'discouragement.'
notes.24:7: The verb venishma (Qal imperfect of shama) literally means "and we will hear" or "listen," carrying the covenantal sense of attentive obedience, placed after "we will do" (naaseh).
notes.24:10: Hebrew livnat hassappir literally refers to brickwork or tiling of sappir, a deep blue gemstone widely identified in antiquity as lapis lazuli rather than modern sapphire.
notes.24:11: Hebrew atsilei ("nobles") is a rare term denoting chief or prominent men; the verb vayyechezu (Qal wayyiqtol of chazah, "gaze upon" or "see in vision") shifts from the ordinary verb raah ("saw") used in verse 10.
notes.24:14: Hebrew baal devarim literally means "owner of words" or "master of matters," an idiom denoting someone who has a legal case or dispute to resolve.
notes.25:5: Hebrew techashim (plural of tachash) is of uncertain meaning; it is commonly linked either to Arabic cognates for marine mammals such as the dugong or dolphin, or to Egyptian and Akkadian terms for fine tanned or beaded leather.
notes.25:9: Hebrew hammishkan ("the tabernacle") literally means "the dwelling place," directly echoing the verb veshakhanti ("and I will dwell," Qal weqatal of shakhan) in verse 8.
notes.25:17: Hebrew kapporet (traditionally rendered "mercy seat") is derived from the root kaphar ("atone" or "cover") and denotes the solid gold lid of the ark that served as the focal place of atonement.
notes.25:28: Hebrew venissa-vam et-hashshulchan illustrates the classical Hebrew construction in which a passive Niphal verb (here Niphal weqatal of nasa, "be carried") retains the direct object marker et before its grammatical subject.
notes.25:33: Hebrew meshuqqadim is a denominative Pual participle derived from shaqed ("almond"), describing cups fashioned in the shape of almonds or almond blossoms.
notes.26:3: The expression rendered 'one to another' is literally the feminine Hebrew idiom 'a woman to her sister' (recurring in 26:5, 6, 17).
notes.26:14: The meaning of the Hebrew plural noun translated 'dugong skins' (techashim) is uncertain; it is variously understood as hides of Red Sea marine mammals such as dugongs or dolphins, or as fine tanned or beaded leather.
notes.26:17: 'Tenons' translates a Hebrew noun literally meaning 'hands' (yadot). The rare Pual participle rendered 'set parallel' (meshullabot) comes from a root associated with rungs or crosspieces, indicating two matched projections aligned with each other.
notes.26:24: The Masoretic text pairs two different terms here: the Qal participle 'doubled' or 'twinned' (to'amim, from ta'am) at the bottom, and the adjective 'complete' or 'whole' (tammim, from tamam) at the top, though some ancient versions read 'twinned' in both places. 'At the top' is literally the distributive singular 'at its top.'
notes.26:34: 'Atonement cover' translates Hebrew kapporet (traditionally 'mercy seat'), derived from the verb root meaning 'to atone' or 'cover' and referring to the golden lid of the ark.
notes.27:3: 'To clear away its ashes' translates a privative Piel infinitive construct (ledashsheno) derived from deshen ('fat-ashes'), meaning to remove the ashes from the altar.
notes.27:7: 'Its poles shall be inserted' renders a 3ms Hophal verb (wehuva') followed by the direct object marker et before the plural noun ('its poles'), an impersonal passive construction common in Biblical Hebrew.
notes.27:8: 'As was shown to you' renders an active 3ms Hiphil verb (her'ah, literally 'one showed you' or 'He showed you') used impersonally, parallel to the Hophal passive in 26:30.
notes.27:18: 'Fifty cubits at each end' translates the Hebrew idiom 'fifty by fifty' (chamishshim bachamishshim), indicating a uniform width of fifty cubits across both the western and eastern ends (see 27:12-13).
notes.28:1: The Piel infinitive construct with a masculine singular suffix (לְכַהֲנוֹ־לִי, literally "for his serving as priest to Me") focuses on Aaron as head of the priesthood even when his sons are named alongside him (compare 28:4, contrasting with the plural Piel verb וְכִהֲנוּ in 28:41).
notes.28:14: The rare term מִגְבָּלֹת (cognate with גַּבְלֻת in 28:22) is paired with מַעֲשֵׂה עֲבֹת ("braided work") and denotes twisted, cord-like craftsmanship, though some interpreters connect it with גְּבוּל ("border/end").
notes.28:17: The precise mineralogical identification of several of the twelve Hebrew gemstone names in 28:17-20 (including פִּטְדָה, יָהֲלֹם, לֶשֶׁם, and תַּרְשִׁישׁ) remains uncertain in modern scholarship; established ancient Near Eastern and standard equivalents are used here.
notes.28:29: In this critical text, 28:29 joins the clauses corresponding to Masoretic 28:24-25 and 28:29 while omitting the material corresponding to Masoretic 28:23 and 28:26-28.
notes.28:41: "Ordain them" renders the Piel idiom וּמִלֵּאתָ אֶת־יָדָם (literally "and you shall fill their hand"), the standard priestly expression for installing and authorizing priests in office.
notes.29:9: Ordain translates the Hebrew idiom meaning literally fill the hand of (Piel of ml' with yad), denoting formal installation into priestly office; the cognate plural noun millu'im (ordination) appears in vv. 22, 26, 27, 31, and 34.
notes.29:27: Hebrew pairs two ritual nouns with their cognate Hophal passive verbs: wave offering (tenufah) with was waved (hunaf, from nuf), and contribution (terumah) with was lifted up (huram, from rum).
notes.29:36: Purify the altar translates the privative Piel of ht' (literally de-sin or purge upon the altar), referring to ritual cleansing from impurity or sin.
notes.29:42: The Masoretic Hebrew shifts from plural you in I will meet with you (lakhem) to singular you in to speak to you (elekha), distinguishing the LORD's meeting with Israel from His direct address to Moses.
notes.29:43: The masculine singular Niphal verb rendered it will be consecrated (niqdash) refers back to the tent of meeting (or the place of meeting) mentioned in v. 42.
notes.30:1: The construct noun miqtar ("burning" or "place of burning," from the root qtr) is a hapax legomenon in the Hebrew Bible, literally rendering the phrase "an altar of the burning of incense."
notes.30:12: "Take a census" translates the Hebrew idiom nasa et-rosh (literally "lift up the head"), used for reckoning a sum or tallying individuals in a muster.
notes.30:25: "A compounded perfume, the work of a perfumer" reflects a triple cognate wordplay on the Hebrew root rqh (roqah mirqahat maaseh roqeah, literally "a perfume of compounding, the work of a perfumer").
notes.30:32: The rare verb form yisakh ("be poured") is a hapax form associated with the roots swk ("anoint, pour oil") or nsk ("pour") and functions with passive sense here.
notes.30:35: "Seasoned with salt" translates the Pual participle memullah (from the root mlh, "to salt"), indicating incense mixed with salt rather than merely blended.
notes.31:10: "The finely woven garments" translates bigde has-serad, containing the rare noun serad (only in Exodus 31, 35, and 39), understood either as plaited or woven work or, following ancient versions, as garments of service.
notes.31:14: "Whoever profanes it" renders a plural Piel participle (mehalleyha, literally "its profaners") paired with a singular Hophal verb (yumat, intensified by the Qal infinitive absolute mot), a distributive Hebrew construction meaning "each one who profanes it shall certainly be put to death."
notes.31:17: "Was refreshed" translates wayyinnapash, the Niphal of npsh (cognate with nephesh, "breath, life, soul"), literally "caught His breath," paired with shavat ("ceased, rested").
notes.32:4: "Shaped it with an engraving tool" translates Hebrew wayyatsar oto bacharet (from tsur II, "fashion, shape," and cheret, "stylus, engraving tool"). Some scholars alternatively read tsur I ("bind up") and cheret ("bag, pouch," cf. 2 Kgs 5:23), yielding "tied it up in a bag."
notes.32:18: The verse plays on two stems of the root anah: the first two occurrences are Qal infinitives construct (anot, "crying out, shouting"), while the third is pointed as a Piel infinitive construct (annot, "singing").
notes.32:24: Hebrew hitparaqu can be parsed either as a Hithpael third-person plural perfect in pause ("they pulled it off"), matching the Masoretic accents, or as a Hithpael masculine plural imperative ("pull it off!") within Aaron's quoted speech.
notes.32:29: "Consecrate yourselves" renders the Hebrew idiom mil'u yedkhem, literally "fill your hand" (here Qal imperative of male'), the standard expression for priestly ordination. The following clause is elliptical, literally "for each man against his son and against his brother."
notes.32:32: Moses' conditional sentence breaks off without a stated conclusion after "if You will forgive their sin" (aposiopesis), leaving the implied relief unspoken in emotional urgency.
notes.33:6: The preposition in mehar Chorev ("from Mount Horeb") has pregnant force, marking the starting point in place and time ("from Mount Horeb on").
notes.33:7: Verses 7-11 use Hebrew imperfect (yiqtol) and waw-consecutive perfect (weqatal) verbs throughout to depict repeated, customary actions in the past ("would take," "would go out," "would speak").
notes.33:14: "My presence" renders Hebrew panay, literally "My face," linking God's promise here and in v. 15 directly to the face imagery of vv. 11, 20, and 23. Hebrew has no words corresponding to "with you" here or in v. 15.
notes.33:19: The double idem per idem construction repeats Qal forms of chanan ("show favor, be gracious") and Piel forms of racham ("have compassion"), expressing God's sovereign freedom in bestowing mercy.
notes.34:5: The verb "proclaimed" (Qal wayyiqtol of qara) has no explicit subject; while the idiom "call on the name of the LORD" often has a human subject, the grammatical continuity of the three verbs in this verse and the promise in 33:19 indicate that the LORD Himself is proclaiming His name.
notes.34:7: Literally "and acquitting He will not acquit" (Piel infinitive absolute with Piel imperfect of naqah), with the object ("the guilty") implied by the context. "Third" and "fourth" translate masculine plural substantives (shilleshim, ribbeim) denoting descendants of the third and fourth generations.
notes.34:19: The rare Masoretic form tizzakar is parsed as a denominative Niphal imperfect from zakar ("male"), meaning "is male" or "is born male"; some scholars revocalize or emend the consonants to hazzakar ("the male").
notes.34:28: The verb "wrote" (Qal wayyiqtol of katav) lacks an explicit subject; grammatically it continues Moses from the preceding clauses and 34:27, though 34:1 and Deuteronomy 10:4 identify the LORD as the One who wrote on the tablets. "The Ten Words" translates aseret haddevarim literally (traditionally known as the Ten Commandments).
notes.34:29: The verb qaran ("was radiant," Qal perfect) is a denominative from qeren ("horn"), used here for emitting rays of light (compare Habakkuk 3:4); the Latin Vulgate's literal rendering "horned" gave rise to traditional depictions of Moses with horns.
notes.35:7: The exact meaning of tehashim (also in 35:23) is uncertain; it is variously understood as finely tanned or beaded leather (comparing Egyptian and Akkadian cognates) or as the hides of a Red Sea marine mammal such as the dugong or dolphin.
notes.35:12: In this Hebrew text, 35:12 combines the furnishings corresponding to traditional MT 35:12, 15, and 17 immediately after the ark and curtain (with no separate verses corresponding to MT 35:8 or 35:18). The noun hatser ("courtyard") takes both a masculine suffix ("its pillars") and a feminine suffix ("its bases") within the same clause.
notes.35:19: The rare term serad ("finely woven") occurs only in Exodus 31:10; 35:19; 39:1, 41; it likely refers to braided or plaited textile work, though ancient versions often understood it as garments for sanctuary service.
notes.35:22: The precise jewelry item denoted by kumaz ("pendants," also in Numbers 31:50) is uncertain, likely gold beads, necklaces, or armbands. "Lifted up a wave offering" renders the Hiphil perfect of nuf with its cognate noun tenufah, denoting a ritual presentation or dedication offering.
notes.36:7: The Hebrew noun melakah ("work") is used twice, first in the extended sense of contributed "material" and then as "work"; wehoter is a Hiphil infinitive absolute of yatar ("to leave over"), used adverbially to express a surplus ("and to spare").
notes.36:8: The rare expression bigde-serad ("woven garments") is of uncertain etymology, variously understood as finely woven or braided textiles or as official garments of service.
notes.36:11: The Ketiv writes the noun with a third-person masculine singular suffix lacking yod (qtswwtw), while the Qere reads the standard plural form qetsotayw ("its ends"), which is translated here.
notes.36:17: The precise mineralogical identification of several of the twelve Hebrew gemstone names in verses 17-20 remains uncertain; the renderings here reflect established lexical and historical identifications.
notes.36:31: The Hophal participle moshzar ("twisted") appears here in the Hebrew text without shesh ("fine linen"), directly modifying the dyed yarns.
notes.37:1: The Hebrew shifts within the verse from a plural Qal wayyiqtol (wayya'asu, "they made") with the collective subject to a singular Qal perfect ('asah, "he made"), referring to the lead artisan Bezalel.
notes.37:16: Literally "height in width" (qomah verohav), reflecting the fact that the vertical height of the hanging corresponded to the woven width of the cloth.
notes.37:17: The Hebrew uses third-person masculine plural possessive suffixes ("their pillars," "their bases") by attraction to the formulaic wording of verses 8-13, although they refer to the singular gate screen of verse 16.
notes.38:5: Hebrew kapporet, traditionally rendered 'mercy seat,' derives from the root k-p-r ('to atone/cover') and denotes the golden lid over the ark associated with atonement.
notes.38:7: Ketiv writes qtswwtw, lacking the yod of the plural possessive suffix, while qere reads the standard plural form qetsotav ('its ends'); both carry the same sense, using a masculine suffix for the grammatically feminine kapporet ('atonement cover').
notes.38:11: The Hebrew source text contains two consecutive pole-making statements—first indefinite ('poles of acacia wood') and then definite ('the poles of acacia wood ... to carry the table')—both rendered directly from the text.
notes.38:26: The Qal participle and perfect of tsava ('to serve/perform assigned duty') describe women performing organized service at the entrance of the tent of meeting; mar'ot denotes polished bronze mirrors.
notes.38:27: The Qal weqatal ('would wash') followed by the Qal yiqtol ('would wash') expresses repeated, customary action whenever Moses, Aaron, and his sons entered the tent or approached the altar.
notes.39:3: A beka is an ancient weight unit equivalent to half a shekel, as the verse immediately explains.
notes.39:8: In this Hebrew text, verse 8 consists of direct-object phrases introduced by the object marker et without a finite verb, while verse 9 supplies the governing verb ('With it he made').
notes.39:18: The exact meaning of Hebrew serad is debated; it is widely connected with plaited, braided, or finely woven fabric, though ancient versions often understood it as 'service garments.'
notes.39:20: The precise meaning of Hebrew techashim is uncertain; scholars variously understand it as fine tanned leather, cognate with Egyptian ths, or dugong/sea-cow hides, cognate with Arabic tukhas.
notes.40:2: The Hebrew phrase literally reads "on the day of the first month," likely referring to the opening new-moon day of the first month, and is immediately specified by "on the first of the month."
notes.40:4: The Hiphil verb from the root alah (literally "cause to go up," also in 40:25) with lamps denotes either lighting them so the flame rises or mounting the detachable oil lamps atop the lampstand.
notes.40:15: The unusual Hebrew idiom combining a finite form of the verb hayah ("to be") with its own infinitive construct (literally "and it shall be to be") expresses enduring appointment: their anointing is to stand for them as an everlasting priesthood.
notes.40:20: The Hebrew term kapporet ("atonement cover") derives from the root kafar ("to atone, cover"), naming the gold lid of the ark as the place of atonement; the traditional rendering "mercy seat" entered English via the Septuagint and Vulgate.
notes.40:35: The Qal verb shakan ("rested, dwelt") plays on the cognate noun mishkan ("tabernacle," literally "dwelling place") at the end of the verse.
